Applications: prototyping (dramatically faster/cheaper than traditional manufacturing), aerospace (GE jet engine fuel nozzles — 5× stronger, 25% lighter than machined), medical (prosthetics, surgical models, custom implants, dental crowns), architecture, fashion, consumer goods. Market: ~$20 billion, projected $100 billion by 2030.

Drones (UAV — Unmanned Aerial Vehicle): remotely piloted or autonomous aircraft. Types: Multirotor (quadcopters, hexacopters — most common for photography/recreation), Fixed-wing (airplane-style — longer range, higher efficiency, used for surveying, military), Hybrid VTOL (vertical takeoff, transitions to fixed-wing for cruise). Key components: flight controller (autopilot computer), ESCs (Electronic Speed Controllers), brushless motors, propellers, LiPo batteries, GPS, IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit). DJI (Chinese company): dominates consumer/prosumer market (~70-80% market share) — Phantom, Mavic, Air, Mini series. FPV (First Person View) racing: pilots wear goggles showing live video, race through gates at 160+ km/h. Military applications: Predator, Reaper (armed UAVs), Bayraktar TB2 (Ukrainian use in 2022 war), kamikaze/loitering munitions (Shahed-136). Commercial: Amazon Prime Air, Wing (Alphabet/Google), Zipline (medical supplies in Rwanda). FAA regulations (USA): Part 107 license for commercial use, registration required >250g, no-fly zones near airports.

Animation history: Eadweard Muybridge (1878) — zoopraxiscope. Émile Reynaud — Praxinoscope (1877), first animated films. Disney (Walt Disney Company, 1923): Snow White (1937, first feature-length cel animation), Fantasia (1940), Bambi (1942). The 'Nine Old Men' — Disney's core animators. Disney Renaissance (1989-1999): The Little Mermaid, Beauty and the Beast, The Lion King, Mulan. Pixar: acquired by Disney 2006 for $7.4B. Toy Story (1995): first feature-length CGI film. Inside Out, WALL-E, Up (critical darlings). Studio Ghibli (Hayao Miyazaki, Japan, 1985): My Neighbor Totoro (1988), Princess Mononoke (1997), Spirited Away (2001, only anime to win Best Animated Feature Oscar). Anime: Japanese animation — enormously diverse genre. Originating from manga (comics). Key studios: Madhouse, MAPPA, Ufotable, Kyoto Animation. Landmark anime: Akira (1988), Ghost in the Shell (1995), Neon Genesis Evangelion (1995-96, TV), Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood, Attack on Titan, Demon Slayer, Dragon Ball Z, One Piece, Naruto. Global anime market: $25+ billion/year.

Modern architecture movements: Bauhaus (1919-1933, Germany, Walter Gropius): 'form follows function' — stripped ornamentation, industrial materials, unified fine arts and crafts. Closed by Nazis. International Style (1920s-60s): glass curtain walls, flat roofs, open plans, Le Corbusier ('a house is a machine for living in'), Mies van der Rohe ('less is more'). Brutalism (1950s-70s): raw concrete (béton brut), massive geometric forms — Boston City Hall, Barbican (London), many Soviet buildings. Postmodernism (1970s-90s): reaction against modernism's austerity — historical references, ornamentation, color, humor. Deconstructivism: fragmented, non-rectilinear forms. Frank Gehry: Guggenheim Bilbao (1997, titanium panels), Walt Disney Concert Hall. Zaha Hadid (first woman to win Pritzker Prize, 2004): fluid, futuristic forms — MAXXI Rome, Guangzhou Opera House. Sustainable architecture: LEED certification, passive house standard (Passivhaus), green roofs, solar integration, net-zero buildings, biophilic design (bringing nature indoors). The Passive House standard achieves 75-90% energy reduction compared to conventional buildings.

Remarkable athletic records: Usain Bolt (Jamaica): 100m world record 9.58s (Berlin 2009, 44.72 km/h average, peak speed ~44.72 km/h) and 200m record 19.19s — both set at the same championships. Michael Phelps: 23 Olympic gold medals, 28 total. Eliud Kipchoge (Kenya): marathon world record 2:00:35 (Berlin 2023). In 2019 (Breaking2, Vienna), ran 1:59:40.2 — but under non-competition conditions (pacers, measured course). World's heaviest bench press: ~503 kg (Julius Maddox, 2023). World's heaviest deadlift: 501 kg (Eddie Hall, 2016) then 501 kg matched and 502.5 kg (Hafþór Björnsson, 2020). High jump world record: 2.45m (Javier Sotomayor, 1993). Long jump: 8.95m (Mike Powell, 1991). Pole vault: 6.22m (Armand Duplantis, 2024, holds multiple WRs). Shot put: 23.37m (Ryan Crouser). Most Grand Slam tennis titles: Novak Djokovic (24+). Most Tour de France wins: 7 (Lance Armstrong — stripped; Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Miguel Induráin each won 5).

Money's evolution: Barter (direct exchange — inefficient, requires 'double coincidence of wants') → Commodity money (shells, grain, cattle — intrinsic value) → Metal coins (Lydian electrum coins, ~600 BC — first standardized coins) → Paper money (China, Tang Dynasty ~7th century AD, called 'flying money'; Europe via goldsmiths' receipts, 17th century) → Central banking (Bank of England 1694 — first modern central bank) → Gold Standard (currency backed by gold — US formally on gold standard 1879-1933 domestically, international gold exchange standard until 1971) → Bretton Woods (1944: currencies pegged to USD, USD pegged to gold at $35/oz — US had 2/3 of world's gold) → Nixon Shock (1971): President Nixon ended USD-gold convertibility → Pure fiat currency (all major currencies today). Interesting fact: the US dollar bill says 'Federal Reserve Note' — it's technically a debt instrument. The Fed can create money by crediting bank accounts. This is how QE (Quantitative Easing) works — central banks create money to buy assets.

Investigative journalism exposes wrongdoing through deep research. Landmark investigations: Watergate (Washington Post, Woodward & Bernstein, 1972-74 — led to Nixon's resignation). Pentagon Papers (NYT/WaPo, 1971 — Daniel Ellsberg leaked secret Vietnam War history, Supreme Court upheld right to publish). Spotlight (Boston Globe, 2001-02 — Catholic Church clergy abuse scandal, ~90 priests in Boston, inspired global investigations, 2015 film). Panama Papers (ICIJ, 2016 — 11.5 million documents from law firm Mossack Fonseca exposing offshore tax havens of world leaders, ~150 media organizations collaborated). WikiLeaks (Julian Assange, 2006): published classified US military and diplomatic documents — Iraq War Logs, Afghan War Diary, diplomatic cables. Controversial: praised as transparency, condemned as endangering lives. Assange arrested in UK, extradition battle with USA. Edward Snowden (NSA contractor, 2013): leaked NSA global surveillance programs (PRISM) to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras. Flew to Russia, lives in exile. Freedom of press: ranked by Reporters Without Borders — Norway #1. USA: #45 (2024). China, North Korea, Eritrea: bottom three consistently.

Consciousness: arguably the hardest problem in science and philosophy. The 'Hard Problem' (David Chalmers, 1995): explaining why there is subjective experience at all — why is there 'something it is like' to be you? (qualia: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain). The 'Easy Problems': explaining cognitive functions (attention, memory, reporting mental states) — not actually easy, but theoretically solvable through neuroscience. Major theories: Global Workspace Theory (Baars, Dehaene): consciousness arises when information is 'broadcast' widely to many brain areas. Integrated Information Theory (Tononi): consciousness is identical to integrated information (Φ). Controversial — implies even simple systems may be conscious. Higher-Order Theories: consciousness requires a representation of one's own mental states. Predictive Processing (Friston, Clark): brain is a prediction machine, consciousness arises from error signals. Free will: compatibilists (free will is compatible with determinism), hard determinists (no free will — all choices are products of prior causes), libertarians (genuine indeterminism enables free will). Libet experiments (1983): brain activity (readiness potential) precedes conscious intention to move by ~350ms — still controversial.

Nuclear fission reactors: uranium-235 or plutonium-239 fuel rods, moderated by water or graphite (slows neutrons to sustain chain reaction), controlled by control rods (absorb neutrons — inserting them slows/stops reaction). Heat generates steam → turbines → electricity. Types: PWR (Pressurized Water Reactor, most common), BWR, CANDU (heavy water), RBMK (Soviet design, used at Chernobyl). Chernobyl disaster (April 26, 1986): RBMK reactor #4 in Ukraine exploded during safety test — design flaw + operator errors. 31 immediate deaths, 4,000-60,000 estimated radiation-related deaths. 30km exclusion zone still exists. Fukushima Daiichi (March 11, 2011): earthquake + tsunami disabled cooling systems → 3 reactor meltdowns. No direct radiation deaths but 2,000+ stress-related deaths from evacuation. Radiation: half-life = time for half of radioactive material to decay. Cesium-137 (30 years), Strontium-90 (29 years), Iodine-131 (8 days), Carbon-14 (5,730 years), Uranium-238 (4.5 billion years). Low-carbon electricity: nuclear produces ~70g CO₂/kWh (lifecycle) vs coal ~820g, gas ~490g, wind ~11g, solar ~40g.

Mental math shortcuts: Multiply by 11: take the number, add its digits, insert the sum between them — e.g., 35×11: 3_5, 3+5=8, answer: 385. Multiply by 9: multiply by 10, subtract the original (9×7 = 70-7 = 63). Square numbers ending in 5: multiply tens digit by (tens digit +1), append 25 — e.g., 35² = 3×4=12, append 25 = 1225. Percentage trick: x% of y = y% of x (e.g., 8% of 25 = 25% of 8 = 2). Estimate square roots: find nearest perfect squares and interpolate. Cast out nines: quick check for arithmetic errors — digits sum to same remainder when divided by 9 for correct calculations. Dividing by 5: multiply by 2, divide by 10. Multiplying by 25: divide by 4, multiply by 100. To check if divisible by 3: sum of digits must be divisible by 3. By 9: sum of digits divisible by 9. By 11: alternating digit sum must be divisible by 11. By 7: complex — double the last digit, subtract from rest, if result divisible by 7, original is too.

Fundamental cooking techniques: Knife cuts: julienne (thin matchsticks 3mm), brunoise (tiny dice from julienne 3mm), dice (small 6mm, medium 12mm, large 20mm), chiffonade (thin ribbon cuts for leaves), mirepoix (rough chop for stocks). Stocks: cold water + bones (roasted for brown stock, unroasted for white/fond blanc) + aromatic vegetables + bouquet garni. Long slow simmer (4-8 hours). Never boil — produces cloudy stock. Sauces — the five mother sauces (Escoffier): Béchamel (butter+flour roux + milk), Velouté (roux + stock), Espagnole/Brown sauce (brown roux + brown stock), Hollandaise (butter emulsified in egg yolks + acid), Tomato. Emulsification: fat dispersed in water (or vice versa) with an emulsifier (lecithin in egg yolks, mustard). Mayonnaise: oil emulsified in egg yolk. Vinaigrette: temporary emulsion. Blanching: briefly boil, then ice bath — preserves color and texture, partially cooks, allows peeling (tomatoes). Deglazing: add liquid to hot pan to lift browned bits (fond) — basis of pan sauces.

Music production: Modern workflow — record/program sounds in a DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) → arrange → mix → master → distribute. DAWs: Ableton Live (electronic music, loop-based), Logic Pro (macOS, popular with pop/hip-hop producers), Pro Tools (industry standard for recording studios), FL Studio (popular with hip-hop producers), GarageBand (free on Mac/iOS), Cubase, Reaper ($60, professional features). Mixing: balancing levels, panning (stereo placement), EQ (equalization — boost/cut frequencies), compression (reduce dynamic range — makes things punchier), reverb (simulate space), delay/echo, stereo widening. The loudness war: over-compression for maximum loudness at expense of dynamics — streaming platforms (Spotify, Apple Music) now use loudness normalization (LUFS standard: −14 LUFS for Spotify, −16 LUFS for Apple Music) — making the loudness war pointless. Mastering: final polish — slight EQ, compression, limiting, ensure consistent playback across systems. Streaming economics: ~$0.003-0.005 per stream on Spotify — need ~250,000 streams to earn minimum wage.

Learning science: Cognitive Load Theory (John Sweller): working memory is limited (~4 items, ~20 seconds without rehearsal). Effective learning manages cognitive load. Spaced repetition: review material at increasing intervals as it becomes stronger in memory — dramatically more effective than massed practice ('cramming'). Anki: flashcard app implementing spaced repetition algorithm. SuperMemo: pioneered the algorithm. The Forgetting Curve (Ebbinghaus, 1885): without review, we forget ~50% in 1 hour, ~70% in 1 day, ~90% in 1 week. Spaced repetition nearly eliminates this. Retrieval practice: testing yourself is more effective than rereading ('the testing effect'). Interleaving: mixing different topics/problem types during practice — feels harder but produces better long-term retention. Elaborative interrogation: ask 'why?' — connecting new info to existing knowledge. The Pomodoro Technique: 25-minute focused work sessions, 5-minute breaks, longer break after 4 sessions. Deliberate practice (Anders Ericsson): focused practice on weaknesses with immediate feedback — basis of expertise development. '10,000 hours' rule is an oversimplification of Ericsson's work.

Silicon Valley culture and startup methodology: Agile software development (2001 Agile Manifesto): iterative development, collaboration, responding to change over following a plan. Scrum: agile framework — 2-week sprints, daily standups, sprint reviews, retrospectives. Roles: Product Owner (defines what to build), Scrum Master (facilitates process), Development Team. Kanban: visualize work on board (To Do → In Progress → Done), limit work in progress (WIP). The Lean Startup (Eric Ries, 2011): Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop. MVP (Minimum Viable Product): simplest version to test hypothesis. Pivot: change direction based on learning. Key SV culture concepts: 'Move fast and break things' (Facebook's old motto — Facebook changed to 'Move fast with stable infrastructure'), 'Fail fast,' 'Default alive vs default dead' (can the startup survive without new fundraising?), 'Product-market fit' (Sean Ellis: would 40%+ of users be 'very disappointed' if product disappeared?). OKRs (Objectives and Key Results): goal-setting framework from Andy Grove at Intel, popularized by John Doerr, used at Google, LinkedIn. '10× thinking': aim 10× better than existing solution, not 10% better. PayPal Mafia: Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, Reid Hoffman, Keith Rabois, Max Levchin — PayPal alumni who went on to found/fund major companies.

Philosophy of science examines the foundations, methods, and implications of science. Scientific method: observation → hypothesis → prediction → experiment → analysis → conclusion. Key concepts: Empiricism: knowledge comes from sensory experience (Bacon, Locke, Hume). Falsifiability (Karl Popper): a theory must be capable of being proven wrong — a hypothesis that can't be falsified is not scientific. Astrology, creationism fail this test. Induction problem (Hume): we can't logically justify inferring general laws from finite observations — the sun has risen every day, but we can't be certain it will tomorrow. Paradigm shifts (Thomas Kuhn, 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions,' 1962): science doesn't progress smoothly — it builds consensus around a paradigm (dominant model), anomalies accumulate, eventually a 'revolutionary' shift replaces the old paradigm (Copernican revolution, quantum mechanics). Normal science vs. revolutionary science. Demarcation problem: what distinguishes science from pseudoscience? No perfect answer. Replication crisis: ~50% of psychology studies fail to replicate in independent tests — questioned the robustness of much published research.

Quantum computing leverages quantum mechanical phenomena for computation. Classical bits: 0 or 1. Qubits: can exist in superposition of 0 AND 1 simultaneously (|0⟩ and |1⟩). Entangled qubits: measuring one instantly determines the state of another regardless of distance. Quantum parallelism: a quantum computer with n qubits can process 2ⁿ states simultaneously. Operations: quantum gates (like logic gates but for qubits). Decoherence: qubits are extremely fragile — any interaction with the environment causes 'decoherence,' destroying quantum state. This is why quantum computers must operate near absolute zero (~15 millikelvin) and why error correction is so critical. Quantum algorithms: Shor's algorithm (1994): factors large integers exponentially faster than classical — would break RSA encryption. Grover's algorithm: searches unsorted database in √N steps vs N. Quantum advantage/'supremacy': Google (2019) claimed a quantum processor performed a task in 200 seconds that would take the best classical supercomputer 10,000 years — disputed by IBM. Major players: IBM (127+ qubit processors, free cloud access), Google (Sycamore, Willow), IonQ, Quantinuum, D-Wave (quantum annealing). Commercial quantum computing: maybe 10-20 years away for practical applications.

Genetics history: Gregor Mendel (Austrian monk, 1856-1863): pea plant experiments revealed inheritance patterns (dominant/recessive alleles, law of segregation, law of independent assortment). Published 1866 — ignored for 35 years. Rediscovered 1900 simultaneously by three scientists. Francis Galton: introduced statistics to biology, coined 'eugenics' (profoundly misused). Thomas Hunt Morgan (1910): established chromosomal theory of heredity using fruit flies — genes on chromosomes. DNA double helix structure: James Watson, Francis Crick, Rosalind Franklin (X-ray crystallography crucial — photo 51), Maurice Wilkins (1953). Watson and Crick used Franklin's data without her knowledge. Nobel Prize 1962 to Watson, Crick, Wilkins — Franklin died in 1958 (Nobels not awarded posthumously). Human Genome Project (1990-2003): mapped all 3 billion base pairs, ~$3 billion cost. Now a genome can be sequenced for ~$200 in days. Whole genome sequencing: identifying every letter of an individual's DNA — transforming medicine (personalized medicine, cancer genomics, rare disease diagnosis, newborn screening). CRISPR-Cas9 (2012 — Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier — 2020 Nobel Prize): precise gene editing.

Podcasting: on-demand audio content, distributed via RSS feeds. Term coined ~2004 (Ben Hammersley suggested 'podcasting' from iPod + broadcasting). iTunes added podcast support 2005 — mainstream arrival. 'Serial' (Sarah Koenig, This American Life spinoff, 2014): first podcast to reach 5 million downloads per episode — sparked true crime podcast boom. Now: 4+ million podcasts, 460+ million listeners worldwide. Major networks: iHeart Media, Spotify (acquired Gimlet, Anchor, Ringer, exclusive deals with Joe Rogan $100M+, Barack Obama, Michelle Obama), NPR, Wondery (Amazon). True crime dominates: Serial, My Favorite Murder, Crime Junkie, Casefile, Dateline. Other huge genres: comedy (My Brother My Brother and Me, How Did This Get Made), news (The Daily, Up First, NPR Politics), interview (Armchair Expert, Smartless, Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend), education (Freakonomics, Radiolab, 99% Invisible), technology (Hard Fork, Acquired, Darknet Diaries). Monetization: ads (~$18-50 CPM), premium subscriptions (Patreon), merchandise. RadioLab, This American Life, Radiolab defined quality long-form audio storytelling.

Literary devices and techniques: Metaphor: direct comparison (life is a journey). Simile: comparison using 'like' or 'as' (fast as lightning). Extended metaphor: sustained metaphor throughout a work. Personification: giving human qualities to non-human things (the wind whispered). Alliteration: repeated initial consonant sounds (Peter Piper picked). Assonance: repeated vowel sounds within words. Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they describe (buzz, crack, hiss). Irony: three types — verbal (saying the opposite of what you mean, often sarcastic), situational (opposite of what's expected happens — a fire station burning down), dramatic (audience knows something characters don't). Foreshadowing: hints at future events. Flashback (analepsis): narrative jumps to the past. Flashforward (prolepsis): narrative jumps to the future. Symbolism: object/action/character represents something beyond its literal meaning. Motif: recurring element that has symbolic significance. Theme: central idea or insight of a work. Allegory: extended narrative where characters and events represent abstract ideas (Animal Farm = Soviet communism). Juxtaposition: placing contrasting elements side by side for effect. Stream of consciousness: writing technique depicting continuous flow of thoughts (James Joyce, Virginia Woolf).

Travel basics: Passports: most powerful (most countries you can visit visa-free) — Japan, Singapore, Germany (190+ countries). US: 186 countries. Weakest: Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan (~30 countries). Visas: some require advance application (India e-Visa, Australian ETA), some issue on arrival, others visa-free based on your passport. Travel insurance: essential — covers medical emergencies (can cost $100,000+ for hospitalization abroad), trip cancellation, lost luggage. Budget travel: hostels ($15-50/night in dorms), house-sitting/Couchsurfing, Airbnb (often cheaper than hotels), overnight trains/buses save hotel costs. Budget airlines: Ryanair (Europe), easyJet, AirAsia (Asia), Southwest (USA). Avoid booking far out for budget airlines (prices fluctuate unpredictably). Travel hacking: credit card points, miles, status — Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum popular. The cheapest times to fly: Tuesday/Wednesday, 5-6 weeks ahead for domestic, 4-6 months ahead for international. Best destinations for budget travelers: Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia), Eastern Europe (Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia), Central America. Colombia and Morocco offer good value.
